Payton Tolle. Ranger Suarez. Sonny Gray.
The Boston Red Sox don’t have to think very long about what their starting rotation should look like for their inevitable wild card matchup with the New York Yankees.
I’ll go and find the numbers to back up this opinion, but before we dive into those let’s just all acknowledge the oldest factor in the book when it comes to these kinds of decisions: the eye test.
Tolle has been a man possessed since the start of August, with seven of his eight outings across that stretch being quality starts and just three of those starts ending before he completed six innings — 48.0 innings pitched, 13 earned runs, 63 strikeouts, 11 walks issued, 2.44 ERA, 2.37 FIP, and one Immaculate Inning.
Suarez shut me right the hell up since your boy had the bright idea of publicly pointing out that he tends to struggle in the month of September. He put up a 4.00 ERA across 168.2 innings pitched in that month throughout the first eight seasons of his career. He’s got a 0.64 across his two starts this month, which isn’t exactly the same sample size but he has been dealing when it matters most.
Gray has also been really good, but he’s clearly starting to strain after carrying the rotation on his back for the majority of the season. The one start he made after receiving extra days rest was superb (7.0 IP, 0R, W). His las start, on normal rest, was rather pedestrian, like the few before he got the breather (6.0, 3R, L).
If you want to talk about how the trio best flows together, it is also important to note where the game is being played and who they’ll be playing against. The Yankees just aren’t as good when they have to deploy their righty-heavy lineup, as it forces guys like Amed Rosario and Heliot Ramos into games over Luis Garcia and Ryan McMahon, and helps limit the overall effectiveness of Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Yankee Stadium has been home to 18 home runs given up by left-handed starting pitchers and 41 home runs given up by right-handed starting pitchers in 2026. If that’s not enough to influence your decision, what is?
Is it the fact that Tolle has the smallest book out on him and has gotten better in August and September? Is it the fact that Suarez has the best postseason pedigree of the three? Is it the fact that Gray notoriously hasn’t pitched well in The Bronx?
I don’t know, man. Tolle in Game 1 of the ALDS sounds pretty damn good to me…

BOSTON (WHDH) - Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle Sunday became just the sixth pitcher in MLB history to throw an immaculate inning in the first inning of a game. An immaculate inning occurs when a pitcher records three strikeouts on nine pitches.
The 23-year-old lefty has quickly become a fan favorite through not only his pitching prowess, but by showcasing his infectious personality. On the eighth pitch of the inning, Tolle flashed a bright smile into the Red Sox dugout before getting Kansas City Royals right fielder Jac Caglianone to strikeout swinging, completing the rare feat.
“We saw him smile towards the end and…said ‘oh my gosh it’s almost immaculate inning,’ and then he got it. And we were just floored,” said Caroline Stacey, a Red Sox fan from Maine. “Tolle is such a great player, he’s so fun to watch. Like, everything he does is just fun so it was really great to see him celebrate and have such an amazing accomplishment.”
The last Red Sox player to throw an immaculate inning at the start of a game was Hall-of-Famer Pedro Martinez in 2002. The then-30-year-old struck out three Mariners in a row on May 18.
“Unbelievable. Eighth in the history of the Red Sox is, I mean, unbelievable,” said Chris Molina, a Red Sox fan visiting Boston from Kansas.
After the game, Tolle said he hopes to ignite the team in any way he can.
“Trying to be the spark in whatever way I can. If that’s pitching or that’s offense, just trying to find that way is kind of what I want to do,” he explained.
It’s that spark that has him winning over the city of Boston as well as his teammates. Red Sox star outfielder Roman Anthony praised Tolle during an on field interview after the game on NESN.
“You see the amount of people that are behind him, and the energy he brings to Red Sox baseball and the city of Boston,” Anthony said. “Everyone around, they ride for him, and we feel that energy when he’s on the bump the minute he takes it. He’s such an amazing person, and an amazing teammate who’s there for us every single day, and whether he’s pitching or not he brings that energy. So it’s so fun to be behind him. He’s amazing.”
The manager of the Red Sox Team Store says they can barely keep his jersey stocked on the shelves as the demand has become so high.
“When you combine the talent that he has with the personality that he has – we’ve seen this before with certain guys like Johnny Damon, David Ortiz, who were big personalities and great players – I mean, that means he’s going to be a star for years to come,” said Tim Pettit, Manager of the Red Sox Team Store.
Following the immaculate inning, Tolle went on to throw five more scoreless innings, finishing with seven strikeouts. The Red Sox went on to beat the Royals 4-1 and secure the series win.

BOSTON — Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle pitched an immaculate inning to open Sunday’s game against the Kansas City Royals.
The 23-year-old left-hander threw a called third strike past Nick Loftin, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the nine-pitch inning.
Tolle became Boston’s first pitcher to throw an immaculate inning opening a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez at Fenway Park against Seattle on May 18, 2002.
“It was pretty cool. It was a pretty cool feeling,” Tolle said after the Red Sox beat the Royals 4-1 to win the series. “That was the first time, I think in high school I might have had a couple of opportunities at it. That was fun, that was cool.”
Caglianone was the only one to get his bat on a ball, fouling his first pitch to the left side.
When Tolle got two strikes on Caglianone, most of the fans rose and cheered loudly. Tolle pumped a fist when the strikeout and inning were complete after looking over at the dugout with a bit of a smile before the last pitch.
“I was definitely thinking about it,” he said. “I looked over at (pitching coach Andrew Bailey) and he was smiling, too.”
It was Boston’s eighth immaculate inning, the second in the first inning and the sixth in MLB recorded history to open the game. Hall of Famer Sandy Koufax had the first recorded one on June 30, 1962.
Chris Sale had the most recent for the Red Sox on Aug. 26, 2021, at Fenway against Minnesota.
Tolle went six scoreless innings with seven strikeouts and allowed four singles.

Los Red Sox tuvieron que retrasar dos veces el inicio del juego del domingo debido a la lluvia que azotó Boston en el cierre de la semana. Fue imposible jugar antes de las 4:55 de la tarde, casi cuatro horas después de lo inicialmente estipulado porque iba a ser un domingo normal con el primer pitcheo lanzándose a la 1:35 de la tarde.
En la medida que se acercaban las 3:00 p.m iba despejándose la duda de que tampoco a esa hora iba a iniciar el duelo entre los patirojos y los Reales de Kansas City. En todo caso, el pitcher Payton Tolle se acercó a su manager Chad Tracy, le hizo un saludo militar y le dijo que estaría listo a la hora que el partido comenzara.
El zurdo no estaba mintiendo. A las 4:55 p.m tiró una recta de 95 millas en strike. Ocho envíos después consiguió una hazaña que solo ocho miembros del club habían conseguido. El monticulista tiró ocho rectas y un sinker para ponchar a sus tres primeros rivales con nueve strikes en fila y convertirse en el octavo miembro de la franquicia en lograr un inning inmaculado.
Es el segundo que lo consigue en el primer inning uniéndose al legendario Pedro Martínez.
“Fue divertido”, celebró Tolle después de la victoria de 4 a 1. “Fue chévere. Creo que después del tercer strike me vino la idea a la cabeza. Pero eso no debería pasar. Creo que debería ser mejor y no andar pensando en esas cosas, pero así sucedió”.
La transmisión del equipo captó el momento previo al último envío antes de la hazaña. Tolle miró a su dugout y sonrió. Dio cuenta que estaba al tanto de lo estaba por suceder en conchupancia con su coach de pitcheo Andrew Bailey.
“Estaba definitivamente pensando en eso”, contó. “Lo tenía en mente. Creo que miré a “Bales” y estaba sonriendo también. Fue divertido”.
Solo ocho monticulistas de los Red Sox habían conseguido esa gesta. El último había sido Chris Sale en mayo de 2021.
“Fue impresionante”, agregó el primera base Willson Contreras, quien regresó a la acción después de casi dos semanas lesionado. “Estuvo atacando la zona de strike. No estaba permitiendo mucha gente en base. Creo que es la primera vez que soy parte de algo así”.
Payton Tolle siguió brillando después de la hazaña y terminó con seis innings completos, sin permitir carreras, un bateador golpeado, cuatro hits y siete ponches.
Y si les quedó alguna duda sobre el saludo militar, tal parece es una broma que se gasta con Tracy todos los días.
“Tiene haciéndolo desde que llegué acá”, bromeó Tracy. “No le pedí que lo hiciera. Solo lo hace. No necesito que lo haga, pero es Tolle y eso es lo que hace”.

Tolle mimics Pedro in immaculate first inning ... with more smiles
This browser does not support the video element.
This story was excerpted from Ian Browne’s Red Sox Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter, click here. And subscribe to get it regularly in your inbox.
BOSTON – It was more than 24 years ago, and I was in my first year covering the Red Sox for MLB.com, and everyone in the press box, the stands and even the two dugouts at Fenway Park were feeling a little restless. That’s what happens when you sit through a two-hour and five-minute rain delay waiting for the game to start.
But Pedro Martínez had a way of making everything worth the wait.
So when Payton Tolle threw his immaculate first inning on Sunday – after a rain delay of nearly two hours – my mind immediately flashed back to May 18, 2002.
Feats like this, these rare milestone moments, are what set baseball apart.
I’ve seen two no-hitters, plus at least four cycles I remember off the top of my head, and countless other unforgettable moments.
The one thing I’ve still never seen live is a perfect game. Here’s hoping I’ll get to witness that someday.
Though I had a scheduled day off on Sunday and wasn’t in my press box perch to witness Tolle becoming the sixth Red Sox pitcher in history to throw an immaculate inning, I immediately flashed back to Martínez against the Mariners on that soggy Saturday nearly a quarter century ago.
Of the eight times on record that Red Sox pitchers have thrown immaculate innings (including three times by Chris Sale), Tolle and Martínez are the only two who started a game by doing so.
Martínez’s day started with the ultimate challenge – facing Ichiro Suzuki. The Seattle hit king was in just his second year stateside, but already a legend.
But he wasn’t ready for Martínez’s first two pitches – a pair of high fastballs which both went for called strikes. The third pitch was a changeup that Suzuki weakly waved through. Seldom had he looked so overmatched on a swing before or after that.
Mark McLemore was up next, and swung through a first-pitch curveball. Then he fouled off a fastball. And looked at a fastball on the outside corner to become Martínez’s second victim.
Ruben Sierra was all that stood between Martínez and what wound up being the only immaculate inning of his Hall of Fame career. Sierra watched a cutter go by for a strike, and looked at a fastball next to make it 0-2.
This browser does not support the video element.
At this point, the Fenway Park crowd stood as one.
“The crowd is standing already, in the first inning,” Red Sox radio play-by-play man Joe Castiglione, a sound of surprise in his voice, informed his audience.
When Martínez got Sierra to fish for a high fastball, the roar was instantaneous.
“That gave us a huge lift,” Boston’s Brian Daubach said after the game. “Running in from left field after the inning, I was like, 'All right, now we’ve got a game.’”
The Red Sox went on to win, 4-1, as Martinez improved to 10-0 against the Mariners with a 0.94 ERA covering 77 innings. Keep in mind that the Mariners of the late 90s and early 2000s were one of the best teams in the game.
While Tolle didn’t face that stiff of an opponent in the Royals, he did go through one of the best players in the game in Bobby Witt Jr. to accomplish his feat. Kansas City’s No. 2 hitter, Witt waved through three straight fastballs between 97 and 98 mph as the second punchout of the first inning.
One of the indelible moments from Tolle’s immaculate frames: the huge grin that spread across his face almost unconsciously between pitches eight and nine. He knew what he was on the verge of doing and soaked in the moment.
Martínez? He never smiled on the mound. He couldn’t compete and have fun at the same time, like Tolle has the unique ability to do.
As different as their personalities are, they are now forever linked in Red Sox history.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

El lanzador zurdo de los Boston Red Sox, Payton Tolle, logró una entrada inmaculada para abrir el partido del domingo contra los Kansas City Royals.
El zurdo de 23 años ponchó a Nick Loftin con un tercer strike cantado y luego retiró a Bobby Witt Jr. y a Jac Caglianone por la vía del strikeout tirándole, todo ello en una entrada de nueve lanzamientos.
Tolle se convirtió en el primer lanzador de Boston en lograr una entrada inmaculada al inicio de un partido desde que lo hiciera el miembro del Salón de la Fama Pedro Martínez en Fenway Park contra Seattle, el 18 de mayo de 2002.
"Fue genial. Fue una sensación increíble", dijo Tolle después de que los Red Sox vencieran a los Royals 4-1 para llevarse la serie. "Fue la primera vez; creo que tal vez tuve un par de oportunidades de lograrlo en la secundaria. Fue divertido, fue genial".
Caglianone fue el único que logró hacer contacto con la pelota, enviando su primer lanzamiento de foul hacia el lado izquierdo.
Cuando Tolle acumuló dos strikes contra Caglianone, la mayoría de los aficionados se puso de pie y vitoreó con fuerza. Tolle celebró con un gesto de puño en alto al concretarse el ponche y finalizar la entrada, tras haber mirado hacia el dugout con una leve sonrisa antes del último lanzamiento.
"Definitivamente estaba pensando en ello", comentó. "Miré hacia donde estaba (el entrenador de lanzadores Andrew Bailey) y él también sonreía".
Fue la octava entrada inmaculada en la historia de Boston, la segunda lograda en el primer episodio y la sexta registrada en la historia de la MLB al inicio de un partido. Sandy Koufax, miembro del Salón de la Fama, protagonizó la primera registrada el 30 de junio de 1962.
Chris Sale había logrado la más reciente para los Red Sox el 26 de agosto de 2021, en Fenway Park y frente a Minnesota.
Tolle lanzó seis entradas en blanco, ponchó a siete bateadores y permitió cuatro sencillos.

Payton Tolle starts with immaculate inning, Roman Anthony gets key hit as Red Sox beat Royals 4-1
The host team defeated the visiting club four to one; the starting pitcher opened the game with an immaculate inning
- 1 minuto de lectura'
BOSTON (AP) — Payton Tolle opened the game with an immaculate inning , Roman Anthony hit a go-ahead single and the Boston Red Sox beat the Kansas City Royals 4-1 on Sunday in a game that’s start was delayed by rain.
Tolle is the first Boston pitcher to throw an immaculate inning (three strikeouts on nine pitches) to start a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did it on May 18, 2002.
Caleb Durbin hit a solo homer and Trevor Story added a game-breaking two-run single for the Red Sox, who took the final two games of the three-game series.
Carter Jensen drove in the Royals’ run with a pinch-hit single. Kansas City was looking for its first series win in Boston since 2017.
In the seventh, Anthony lined an opposite-field single against reliever Connor Thomas after Craig Kimbrel (1-5) walked the first two batters.
Garrett Whitlock (7-1) was credited with the victory. Aroldis Chapman got the final three outs for his 34th save and the 401st of his career.
Tolle, a hard-throwing 23-year-old left-hander, fanned Nick Loftin called, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the first.
He went six scoreless innings, striking out seven while allowing four singles.
Noah Cameron gave up a run over six sharp innings.
Durbin belted Cameron’s first pitch into the first row of seats above the Green Monster. Story’s single came off Nate Pearson in the eighth.
Jensen’s RBI single inside the first-base bag tied it.
The club announced Saturday that the finale's start time was pushed back 90 minutes due to the forecast of rain, which came and delayed the first pitch by 1 hour, 50 minutes.

Royals: RHP Michael Wacha (9-8, 3.25 ERA) is scheduled for the opener of a three-game series in Houston on Tuesday.
Red Sox: LHP Patrick Sandoval (1-5, 4.58) starts Tuesday in the series opener against Texas.
